after.title: DOJ sues Anne Arundel school board over parental access and student gender policies
after.dek: The eight-count federal complaint seeks declarations and injunctions under FERPA and PPRA; the district denies violating either law.
facts: The United States filed an eight-count complaint against the Board of Education of Anne Arundel County in Maryland federal court on October 27, case 1:26-cv-04499-CJC. The stamped original establishes a filed enforcement case, not a judicial finding.

DOJ alleges that the district’s Regulation JQ-RA and handling of student names, pronouns, gender information and education records violate parental rights under the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act and Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment. These are disputed legal and factual allegations; this record does not reproduce the complaint’s account of an individual minor.

The complaint requests declarations of violations and an injunction against noncompliant policies and practices, with record-review and correction procedures and parental-consent or opt-out protections for specified student inquiries. Requested relief is not an issued injunction, a verified funding cutoff or an implemented nationwide school rule.

DOJ describes the action as protecting parents’ access to records and participation in decisions concerning their children. Reuters reports that the district disputes the allegations, maintains it complies with FERPA and PPRA, and says litigation followed good-faith discussions.
after.significance: The filing uses federal enforcement power to contest how a public school system handles student information and parental access. Its reach and consequences depend on the statutes, record and court decisions, not DOJ’s announcement alone.
after.goalpost: DOJ’s strongest case is that parents have enforceable access, correction and consent rights that district practices cannot override. The district’s documented response is that it complies with both laws. Actual policy text, the factual record and judicial interpretation are the tests.
after.maybe_therefore: Maybe the case enforces valid parental-record rights, or an overbroad interpretation intrudes on lawful student-privacy practices. Therefore this is a disputed enforcement filing, not proof of illegal conduct, medical treatment, established harm or a new national mandate.
after.evidence: Original 31-page complaint: caption, opening allegations, count headings and prayer inspected; DOJ release and independent Reuters reporting with district response. Filed/pending; October 27 recovery, not an action first occurring after the current cutoff opened.
institutions: U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland
Anne Arundel County Board of Education

after.title: Reported ruling disqualifies Essayli from two prosecutions, with enforcement delayed
after.dek: AP and the Daily Journal report a new appointment-authority ruling; it does not establish immediate removal or dismissal of prosecutions.
facts: AP and the Daily Journal report that Judge J. Michael Seabright ruled October 27 that Bill Essayli was unlawfully serving as de facto U.S. attorney despite first-assistant and special-attorney designations.

The Daily Journal identifies disqualification from participating in or supervising the Ramirez and Tran prosecutions. Enforcement is postponed for a government stay request. The original order was not retrieved, so this record asserts no exact operative deadline.

The Los Angeles Times reports the indictments were not dismissed. AP reports Essayli disagrees and defends presidential and attorney-general authority to select DOJ supervisors while anticipating Supreme Court review.
after.significance: The reported ruling tests executive control of a major prosecution office through delegated titles rather than Senate confirmation. It does not automatically invalidate other prosecutions.
after.goalpost: Essayli’s documented defense is executive authority to choose DOJ supervisors. The scope and legality of delegation remain contested through the stay and appellate process; an anticipated Supreme Court decision is not an existing ruling.
after.maybe_therefore: Maybe lawful delegation supports continuity, or it evades appointment limits. Therefore the finding is a reported, narrowly scoped disqualification with delayed enforcement, not completed removal or nationwide invalidation.
after.evidence: AP and Daily Journal original reporting, with brief Los Angeles Times confirmation. Named judicial ruling as reported; primary order uninspected. Earlier-date recovery; AP publication was October 28 at 04:36:45 UTC, before the new window.
institutions: U.S. District Court for the Central District of California
